content: 1. Increasing HIV testing coverage among children aged two years and older who have been exposed to HIV is particularly important. Some programs are currently evaluating the use of oral fluid-based rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) administered by trained lay providers to improve the acceptability and feasibility of testing in this population. However, it is critical to ensure that children being tested are not already on treatment or enhanced postnatal prophylaxis regimens. 2. Less than one-third of infants infected perinatally are linked to services and initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) in a timely manner. Routine offering of HIV testing services (HTS) remains a key strategy for identifying HIV in infants and children, particularly in high HIV burden settings. This is especially important for HIV-exposed, sick, or hospitalized children. 3. In high HIV burden settings, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends routine facility-based HTS for infants and children with unknown HIV status who are admitted for inpatient care or attending malnutrition clinics. WHO also suggests offering HTS to infants and children with unknown HIV status in outpatient or immunization clinics in these settings. 4. Risk-based screening tools or questionnaires for older children can increase the number of children receiving HIV testing. These tools can prompt providers to offer testing to children with specific HIV risks or indicator conditions who might otherwise be overlooked. 5. For example, in Nigeria, where routine HTS for older children is not provided, the introduction of a validated screening tool increased testing coverage among sick and hospitalized children by 27% and the number of newly diagnosed HIV cases by 36%. However, in high HIV burden settings, tools designed to screen out those in need of testing may not be appropriate, as they could be misused, deter uptake, and miss children requiring testing. 6. WHO recommends routine facility-based HTS in inpatient care and malnutrition clinics for infants and children with unknown HIV status in high HIV burden settings. Infants and children with unknown HIV status should also be offered testing in outpatient or immunization clinics in these settings. 7. Adding nucleic acid testing (NAT) at birth to existing early infant diagnosis (EID) testing approaches can be considered to identify HIV infection in HIV-exposed infants. NAT technologies validated for use at or near the point-of-care can also be used for early infant HIV testing. 8. HIV virological testing should be used to diagnose HIV infection in infants and children below 18 months of age. All HIV-exposed infants should undergo virological testing at 4–6 weeks of age or at the earliest opportunity thereafter. 9. For infants with an initial positive virological test result, ART should be initiated without delay, and a second specimen should be collected to confirm the initial positive result. Immediate initiation of ART saves lives and should not be delayed while awaiting confirmatory test results. 10. Test results from virological testing in infants should be returned to the clinic and caregiver as soon as possible, but no later than four weeks after specimen collection. Positive test results should be fast-tracked to enable prompt initiation of ART. 11. All infants with unknown or uncertain HIV exposure seen in healthcare facilities at birth, the first postnatal visit (usually 4–6 weeks), or other child health visits should have their HIV exposure status determined. 12. HIV-exposed infants who are well should undergo serological testing at around nine months of age (or at the time of the last immunization visit). Infants with reactive serological assays at nine months should have a virological test to confirm HIV infection and determine the need for ART. 13. Infants with signs or symptoms suggestive of HIV infection should undergo serological testing, and if positive, virological testing should be performed. 14. Children aged 18 months or older with suspected HIV infection or exposure should have serological testing performed according to the standard diagnostic HIV testing algorithm used in adults. 15. Biological children of a parent living with HIV (or who may have died of HIV) should be routinely offered HTS. If found to be infected or at high risk of infection through breastfeeding, they should be linked to services for treatment or prevention and offered a broader package of voluntary provider-assisted referral. 16. National regulatory agencies are encouraged to adopt point-of-care EID without delay by streamlining registration and approval processes for immediate implementation. 17. Testing partners of people with HIV is an effective way to reach individuals at high risk of HIV infection. This approach efficiently identifies additional people with HIV who are not yet diagnosed or on ART, particularly male partners in high HIV burden settings who are less likely to test than women. 18. Partner testing also facilitates linkage to prevention interventions, such as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), safer conception, or contraception. It can improve ART adherence among HIV-positive partners and support prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) among HIV-positive pregnant women. 19. Couples and partner HTS must be voluntary and not forced. Providers must recognize that some clients may not want to involve their partners. Couples and partners from key populations or in serodiscordant relationships should be prioritized. 20. Serodiscordance is common among couples, with one partner being HIV-positive and the other negative in up to two-thirds of cases. However, many people are unaware of their partner’s HIV status. Few couples test together, even in countries where partner testing is included in national policy. 21. WHO recommends provider-assisted referral as a preferred approach to support partner testing as part of a voluntary comprehensive care package. This involves a trained provider offering HTS to sexual and drug-injecting partners with the consent of the index client. 22. HIV self-testing (HIVST) is a safe, acceptable, and effective way to reach partners of HIV-negative antenatal care clients and partners of people diagnosed HIV-positive at facilities. Social network-based approaches can also promote HTS among sexual and drug-injecting partners and social contacts of key populations. 23. Programs should offer options based on client preferences, such as how partners could be contacted (e.g., by phone, social media, or home visit). However, provider-assisted referral should be prioritized whenever possible due to its effectiveness. 24. Testing biological children of people with HIV whose status is unknown should be considered as part of a voluntary provider-assisted referral package. Providers must offer information to couples and partners, particularly those with serodiscordant status, to understand their results and provide the latest information on HIV prevention, treatment, and reproductive health options. 25. Partner testing, whether together or separately, is recommended with support for mutual disclosure where beneficial. Care must be taken to minimize the risk of partner violence. Providers should discuss the potential benefits and risks of disclosure, including the possibility of violence, and offer options for safe disclosure. 26. Women who fear or are experiencing violence should undergo safety assessment and planning. Options include mediated disclosure, delayed disclosure, or deciding not to disclose if there is a risk of severe violence. 27. Training for HTS providers should include how to discuss and respond to the potential for violence and ensure that people experiencing violence receive care and support. Discussions with women should focus on whether they foresee a potential for intimate partner violence (IPV). 28. Tools are available to help women assess the potential for violence based on their partner’s past behavior. If a woman has experienced violence by her current partner in the past, the likelihood of violence upon disclosure of her HIV-positive status is heightened. 29. Members of key populations, regardless of gender, may also be at risk of violence when disclosing their HIV-positive status. Discussions about this possibility should be part of disclosure planning. 30. WHO recommends that interventions supporting women with HIV considering voluntary disclosure include discussions about their current situation, the associated risks of violence, and actions to disclose more safely. Links to violence prevention and care services should also be facilitated. 31. For those disclosing sexual abuse within five days of its occurrence, clinical care should include first-line support, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) within 72 hours, STI prophylaxis or presumptive treatment, emergency contraception within 120 hours, and access to safe abortion as permitted by law. 32. Women disclosing any form of violence by an intimate partner or sexual assault by any perpetrator should be offered immediate support.
